title: Site overview
text:
1. The Harborwick warehouse provides a single enclosed floor covering 6,000 m2 for receiving, storage, picking, packing and dispatch under one roof.
2. Circulation inside the building separates mechanical handling routes from segregated footways so equipment and pedestrians remain apart at all times.
3. All personnel entering the operations floor shall orient themselves using the posted site plan before proceeding beyond the entrance lobby.
4. Main transport aisles are 4.0 m wide and carry two-way traffic for forklifts, reach trucks and pallet jacks between functional areas.
5. Rack storage aisles are 3.0 m wide and serve single-aisle access to high-bay racking for put-away and replenishment movements.
6. Segregated pedestrian walkways are 1.2 m wide and are physically marked to keep foot traffic clear of handling equipment.
7. Eight dock doors serve the building perimeter and connect internal staging areas directly with the outdoor yard.
8. Every dock approach shall be kept clear of pallets, waste and loose packaging to preserve sight lines for reversing vehicles.
9. Pedestrians shall use only the marked walkways and crossings when moving between the entrance, offices and operational areas.
10. Drivers reporting for loading or unloading shall follow yard signage and wait at the designated holding position until called forward.
11. Visitors without induction shall remain with their escort and stay within the walkways throughout their time on site.
12. Marked crossings define the only permitted points for stepping across a transport aisle or a dock approach.
13. Keep to the right-hand side of walkways and aisles where directional arrows are painted.
14. Never obstruct a main transport aisle, a rack storage aisle or a walkway with staged goods, idle equipment or refuse.
15. When moving through intersections, establish eye contact with equipment operators before stepping into the shared line of sight.
16. Use high-visibility routes at night and during low-light operations without deviating onto unmarked shortcuts.
17. Report faded floor markings, damaged barriers or blocked sight lines to supervision immediately for reinstatement.
18. Crossing between racking rows shall take place only at aisle ends and never through the racking structure itself.
19. Warehouse lighting, ventilation and floor surfaces support continuous handling while preserving the stated clear widths for safe passage.
20. Forklift and pedestrian paths intersect only at signed crossings where walkway continuity is maintained across the wider transport corridor.
21. Yard movements feed the eight doors without requiring vehicles or pedestrians to cross unrelated work zones.
22. Storage of goods outside marked bays is prohibited where it would reduce the available width of any transport aisle or walkway.
23. Temporary closures of aisles or walkways require barriers, diversion signs and communication to affected teams before work begins.
24. Familiarity with the 6,000 m2 footprint, the 4.0 m main aisles, the 3.0 m storage aisles, the 1.2 m walkways and the eight dock doors forms the basis for safe movement across the site.

title: Zones A-F
text:
1. Zone A is the receiving zone: inbound docks 1-4, unloading and goods inspection. All inbound vehicles report to Zone A and remain at the assigned dock until released. Unloading, counting and inspection take place inside Zone A before any goods move further into the warehouse.

Segregation between inbound and outbound traffic starts at the dock wall. No outbound staging or loading takes place in Zone A. Equipment for unloading is staged along the Zone A wall to keep the dock approaches clear.

2. Zone B is the bulk storage zone: high-bay pallet racking. The high-bay racking provides 2,400 pallet positions for reserve and bulk stock. Only palletised reserve stock is held in Zone B, with ground-level pick faces held separately in Zone C.

Put-away from Zone A feeds directly into Zone B locations under system direction. Replenishment to the pick faces draws from Zone B reserve positions. Access within Zone B follows the marked rack storage aisles.

3. Zone C is the picking zone: ground-level pick faces and flow racks. Customer orders are picked in Zone C against scanner tasks at the ground-level locations. Flow racks in Zone C provide gravity feed for small units and fast movers.

Replenishment keeps the Zone C faces filled from Zone B before picking starts. Empty pallets and packaging waste are removed from Zone C during the shift to keep pick aisles passable.

4. Zone D is the dispatch zone: outbound staging in front of docks 5-8. Packed and labelled consignments are staged by load in Zone D in dock-door order. Each staged load remains with its documentation until loading is called.

Loading takes place only through docks 5-8 from Zone D. No receiving, inspection or long-term storage takes place in Zone D. Cleared staging lanes are reset immediately after each trailer departs.

5. Zone E is the cold zone: chilled storage held at +2 to +8 °C. Chilled products remain in Zone E from booking until picking or dispatch. Doors to Zone E stay closed except for goods movements to protect temperature control.

Temperature monitoring and manual verification cover Zone E on every shift. Any pallet found outside its permitted temperature range is moved to quarantine for assessment.

6. Zone F holds the value-added services area. Packing rework, labelling, kitting and other customer-specific tasks are carried out in Zone F. The quarantine area is in Zone F for suspect, damaged or temperature-affected stock awaiting a decision.

Returns are inspected in Zone F, where staff propose restock, rework or scrap for approval. The hazmat cage is inside Zone F and covers 60 m2 for segregated storage of hazardous materials.

Movement between zones follows the marked main transport aisles and pedestrian walkways. Pallets transfer from Zone A to Zone B, Zone B to Zone C, Zone C to Zone D, with Zone E and Zone F linked by the same aisle system for their specific goods flows.

title: Docks and yard
text:
1. The building has 8 dock doors in a single straight run along the dock face. Keep the full set available for scheduled arrivals and departures and keep the apron and approach lanes clear at all times.

All doors are numbered consecutively from one end of the building to the other. Use only the painted door numbers for bookings, assignments and radio communication. Do not use informal names for doors.

2. Dock doors 1-4 serve inbound receiving. Direct every inbound curtain-side trailer and delivery vehicle reporting for unloading to doors 1-4 only.

Zone A is the receiving zone: inbound docks 1-4, unloading and goods inspection. Hold inbound pallets, unloading equipment and inspection records inside Zone A until booking and release are complete. Do not stage inbound goods in front of the outbound doors.

3. Dock doors 5-8 serve outbound dispatch. Direct every outbound trailer and van reporting for loading to doors 5-8 only.

There are 4 outbound dock doors. Zone D is the dispatch zone: outbound staging in front of docks 5-8. Build and stretch-wrap outbound loads in the Zone D staging lanes and call forward transport only when the load is released.

4. The dispatcher assigns dock doors and time slots to carriers. Request a door and slot before arrival and wait for confirmation.

Issue the following instructions with every assignment:
1) confirmed door number within the correct inbound or outbound range;
2) confirmed arrival window and reporting point;
3) contact name and channel for arrival and delays.

Do not change an assigned door without dispatcher approval. Record every change against the original booking so the yard sequence remains traceable.

5. Each of the 8 dock doors has a dock leveller. Deploy the leveller only after the vehicle is braked, chocked and confirmed stationary at the door.

Operate levellers in this order:
1) check the leveller, dock edge and approach for damage or obstruction;
2) position and extend the leveller lip fully onto the vehicle bed;
3) confirm stable seating before starting forklift or pallet-jack movements.

Report bent lips, failed hydraulics, missing chocks or door faults immediately and take the affected door out of service until repaired. Never bridge a gap with pallets, boards or other makeshift material.

6. Manage the yard as one controlled area serving both door ranges. Separate inbound queuing from outbound loading queues and hold waiting vehicles clear of the dock approaches.

Enforce the following yard discipline:
1) inbound vehicles wait for release to doors 1-4 and then proceed directly to the assigned door;
2) outbound vehicles wait for release to doors 5-8 and remain clear of the staging lanes until called;
3) keep pedestrian routes, dock ramps and leveller approaches free of parked equipment, pallets and waste.

Coordinate late arrivals, door conflicts and equipment failures through the dispatcher so inbound receiving and outbound dispatch continue without cross-use of doors.

title: Management and supervision
text:
1. The warehouse manager is accountable for the whole site: operations, safety and final sign-offs. That accountability covers daily throughput, compliance with site rules, and coordination across all shifts. No operational decision overrides that overall responsibility.

2. During their assigned hours, the shift supervisor runs one shift: floor staff and incident response. Direction of inbound, storage, picking and dispatch tasks on the floor sits with the supervisor on duty. Escalation from operators goes to that supervisor in the first instance.

3. Authority for PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts rests with the warehouse manager at sign-off stage. Only the warehouse manager may sign off stocktake results. Stock controllers prepare counts and recounts, supervisors support execution, but results remain draft until that sign-off is recorded.

4. Under PR-09 Damaged-goods handling, financial control for larger losses stays at management level. The warehouse manager approves damaged-goods write-offs above 500 EUR. Lower-value cases follow the separate supervisor route, while any case above that threshold waits for management approval.

5. Control of working hours beyond the rostered pattern is centralised for cost and fatigue management. Only the warehouse manager may approve overtime. Supervisors identify the need and submit the request, without committing extra hours before approval is granted.

6. Competence control for powered equipment remains a management prerogative under PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation. Only the warehouse manager may authorise new forklift operators. Authorisation follows completion of the required training and assessment, and unauthorised operators must not be assigned to trucks.

7. Immediate response on the floor belongs to the shift supervisor on duty. The shift supervisor reviews every incident report. That review checks facts, identifies immediate safeguards, and forwards matters needing management decision or external notification to the warehouse manager.

8. In practice the two roles divide by horizon and scope. Supervisors allocate people, sequence tasks within the shift, and contain incidents as they occur. The warehouse manager sets priorities between functions, resolves conflicts over resources, and provides the final sign-offs on stocktake, high-value write-offs, overtime and forklift authorisations.

9. Handover between management and supervision keeps accountability continuous across shift changes. Outgoing supervisors brief the incoming supervisor and flag open incidents, pending approvals and risks to the plan. Matters reserved for the warehouse manager remain open until that manager decides, with interim containment owned by supervision.

title: Operational roles
text:
1. Forklift operators operate forklifts, reach trucks and pallet jacks.
Deployed across receiving, storage, replenishment and dispatch tasks, forklift operators move pallets only against WMS instructions and confirmed dock assignments.
Coordinated by the shift supervisor during PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation, forklift operators yield to pedestrians, observe posted limits and complete the daily pre-use check before first use.

2. Pickers pick customer orders in Zone C against scanner tasks.
Assigned to ground-level pick faces and flow racks, pickers follow the replenishment sequence under PR-03 Replenishment of pick faces so faces are filled before the picking shift starts.
Verified through scan confirmation under PR-04 Order picking, pickers place picked items for PR-05 Packing and labelling without substituting products or quantities.

3. Inbound operators unload, count and inspect inbound goods in Zone A.
Stationed at dock doors 1-4, inbound operators execute PR-01 Inbound receiving by checking documents before unloading and inspecting goods before system booking.
Released pallets transfer onward from Zone A to Zone B to Zone C to Zone D only after booking, with exceptions segregated immediately for stock-controller review.

4. Stock controllers own inventory accuracy: cycle counts, recounts and adjustments.
Working daily on a rotating zone schedule, stock controllers perform cycle counts across Zone B racking, Zone C pick faces, Zone E and the Zone F quarantine area.
Governed by PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts, stock controllers require a second count before any adjustment is posted and submit results for warehouse-manager sign-off.

5. Returns staff inspect returns in Zone F and propose restock, rework or scrap.
Located at the returns inspection point, returns staff apply PR-07 Returns handling and accept returns within the permitted window, inspecting condition, quantity and temperature status where relevant.
Documented proposals distinguish restock to Zone B or Zone C, rework in Zone F, or scrap, with final disposition subject to shift-supervisor approval before any movement.

6. Maintenance technicians sustain equipment availability and safety compliance.
Within this site the maintenance technician maintains MHE, racking and dock equipment and logs all repairs.
Covering electric counterbalance units, reach trucks, pallet jacks, stretch wrappers, levellers and racking, maintenance technicians isolate defective equipment, record interventions in the repair log and trigger monthly racking inspections.

7. Dispatchers book transport, assign dock doors and release outbound loads.
Acting as scheduling owner, the dispatcher assigns dock doors and time slots to carriers and stages outbound work in front of docks 5-8.
Executed under PR-06 Outbound dispatch, dispatchers confirm trailer readiness, authorise loading in the prescribed leveller order and release only complete, documented loads for departure.

title: Approvals and sign-offs
text:
1. Submit all stocktake results to the warehouse manager for sign-off.
Only the warehouse manager may sign off stocktake results under PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts. Shift supervisors coordinate counters and recounts on the floor, stock controllers prepare adjustments for review, but neither role may close the count. Withhold system posting until written sign-off is recorded.

2. Escalate damaged-goods write-offs above 500 EUR to the warehouse manager.
Damaged-goods write-offs above 500 EUR need warehouse-manager approval under PR-09 Damaged-goods handling. Attach photographs, WMS records and the inspection note to the request. Do not scrap, discount or adjust stock before approval is granted.

3. Obtain shift-supervisor approval for damaged-goods write-offs up to 500 EUR.
The shift supervisor approves damaged-goods write-offs up to 500 EUR. Present the damaged stock, value calculation and proposed action during the shift. Record the decision, approver name and time in the damage log before moving goods to quarantine or scrap.

4. Route every inspected return through the shift supervisor for disposition.
The shift supervisor approves the final disposition of inspected returns under PR-07 Returns handling. Returns staff propose restock, rework or scrap after inspection in Zone F. Release restock to Zone B or Zone C, rework to the value-added services area, or scrap only after the disposition is signed.

5. Request overtime exclusively from the warehouse manager.
Only the warehouse manager may approve overtime. Shift supervisors forecast workload, identify shortfalls in picking, receiving or dispatch, and submit hours, dates and reasons in advance. Do not work additional hours until approval is confirmed and rostered.

6. Book all dock activity through the dispatcher.
The dispatcher assigns dock doors and time slots to carriers under PR-01 Inbound receiving and PR-06 Outbound dispatch. Carriers receive a numbered door and scheduled window before arrival. Inbound operators and dispatchers sequence unloading and loading to that plan and report conflicts back to the dispatcher for reallocation.

7. Forward each incident report to the shift supervisor for review.
The shift supervisor reviews every incident report, covering safety events, near misses, equipment damage and operational failures. Initiate the report immediately after making the area safe and notifying supervision. Implement corrective actions only as directed in the review and retain the closed report on file.

8. Nominate new forklift operators solely to the warehouse manager for authorisation.
Only the warehouse manager may authorise new forklift operators under PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation. Candidates complete training, assessment and licence verification before nomination. Prohibit solo operation of forklifts, reach trucks and pallet jacks until written authorisation is issued.

title: Shift pattern
text:
1. Operate the site on a two-shift pattern from Monday to Friday.
2. Staff Shift 1 from 06:00-14:00, Monday to Friday.

Shift 1 opens the building, starts inbound receiving and picking, and carries out morning checks. Complete all planned tasks before the shift change and prepare work in progress for transfer.

3. Staff Shift 2 from 14:00-22:00, Monday to Friday.

Shift 2 continues picking, replenishment and outbound dispatch, closes open tasks, and secures the site at the end of the day. Do not extend work beyond 22:00 without approved overtime.

4. Assign one shift supervisor to each shift.

The shift supervisor runs one shift: floor staff and incident response. Keep that accountability visible on the shift roster and on the floor during working hours.

5. Publish the weekly roster before the working week starts.

Show names, roles and shift allocation for both shifts. Record planned absences and arrange cover within the existing shifts before requesting additional hours.

6. Hand over between shifts at 14:00 every working day.

Use PR-15 End-of-shift handover for the transfer between Shift 1 and Shift 2. Include open inbound loads, replenishment status, order progress, equipment faults, staffing gaps and safety issues.

7. Require the outgoing shift supervisor to brief the incoming shift supervisor face to face.

Confirm priorities for the next eight hours, agree labour allocation, and sign the handover record. Escalate unresolved problems rather than carrying them forward silently.

8. Keep overtime as an exception, not as planned cover.

Only the warehouse manager may approve overtime. Request approval before working extra hours, record the reason and duration, and retain the approval with the roster.

9. Prohibit self-authorised overtime by any other role.

Direct all requests through the shift supervisor to the warehouse manager. Do not work beyond 06:00-14:00 or 14:00-22:00, Monday to Friday, unless approval is confirmed.

10. Monitor hours, fatigue and handover quality across both shifts.

Adjust task allocation when workload peaks, rotate demanding duties within the shift, and review repeated overtime requests for root causes in planning or staffing.

title: End-of-shift handover
text:
1. Apply PR-15 End-of-shift handover on every change of shifts without exception.
2. Shift 1 runs 06:00-14:00, Monday to Friday, and Shift 2 runs 14:00-22:00, Monday to Friday.
3. Shift handover between Shift 1 and Shift 2 occurs at 14:00 every working day.
4. One shift supervisor is assigned to each shift.
5. The shift supervisor runs one shift: floor staff and incident response.
6. Hold accountability for the floor continuously through the handover point.
7. Under PR-15 End-of-shift handover, record staffing present, tasks in progress, equipment status and open incidents.
8. Before the handover meeting, walk the floor and confirm the state of receiving, storage, picking and dispatch areas.
9. Note any blocked aisles, idle handling equipment, delayed loads or incomplete replenishment for the incoming shift.
10. During the meeting, brief outstanding inbound, put-away, picking and outbound work face to face.
11. The outgoing shift supervisor must brief the incoming shift supervisor face to face and sign the handover record.
12. Jointly sign the handover record only when both supervisors accept the stated floor position.
13. Never leave the floor unattended during the handover discussion.
14. Carry open incident reports into the next shift with a named owner and agreed next action.
15. The shift supervisor reviews every incident report.
16. On nights or at week end, ensure the outgoing supervisor reviews all incident reports raised during the shift.
17. Direct the incoming supervisor to any witness statements still missing, areas still cordoned off, or equipment still quarantined.
18. Instruct the incoming team on changed priorities, hazards found, and follow-up checks required.
19. Pass on the status of dock activity, labour allocation and pending arrivals or departures.
20. Confirm which zones need immediate attention at shift start to protect service and safety.
21. File the signed handover record where the next supervisor, auditor or manager can retrieve it without delay.
22. Escalate immediately if the incoming shift supervisor cannot be contacted, if staffing is unsafe, or if an unresolved incident prevents normal operation.
23. Treat an unsigned or incomplete handover as an open risk and remain accountable until a proper briefing is completed.

title: Per-shift checks
text:
Complete the following checks on every shift. The shift supervisor runs one shift: floor staff and incident response, and remains accountable for confirming each check is finished before handover.

1. Confirm shift cover and start position. Shift 1 runs 06:00-14:00, Monday to Friday. Shift 2 runs 14:00-22:00, Monday to Friday. Verify attendance against the weekly roster, reassign scanners and MHE, and walk receiving, storage, picking and dispatch areas to establish the opening position.

2. Manually verify cold-zone temperature each shift. Enter Zone E and read the calibrated display for the chilled storage held at +2 to +8 °C. Record the reading in the temperature log with time and initials. Act without delay under PR-12 Cold-chain handling if the reading is outside range, if the display is blank, or if the door has been left open.

3. Inspect Zone E stock at risk during the same visit. Check for ice build-up, standing water, open cartons and pallets left in the doorway. Move any pallet found outside permitted temperature range to quarantine for assessment only through the defined route, and notify the next supervisor of any hold.

4. Review inventory tasks with stock control. Stock controllers own inventory accuracy: cycle counts, recounts and adjustments. Obtain the rotating count plan for the day, confirm which locations are released for counting, and keep counted locations clear of put-away and picking until the count is closed.

5. Execute counts under PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts. Direct pickers and inbound staff to pause movements in the count area, require a second count before any adjustment is posted, and escalate blocked locations, damaged labels and system mismatches to the stock controller the same shift.

6. Check floor safety and equipment availability. Confirm pedestrian walkways are clear, dock levellers are parked, spill kits are in place, and sufficient handheld scanners and pallet jacks are charged for the shift workload. Remove defective equipment from service and report faults for logging and repair.

7. Review open incidents, returns and exceptions. Check the incident log for events carried over from the previous shift, verify that returns segregation and quarantine decisions are progressing, and ensure inbound exceptions are held for stock-controller review rather than booked or put away.

8. Close the shift with PR-15 End-of-shift handover. Update the handover record with temperature results, count progress, equipment defects and outstanding incidents. Brief the incoming team face to face so the next shift starts from a verified floor position.

title: Arrival and scheduling
text:
1. Process every inbound delivery in Zone A under PR-01 Inbound receiving.

2. Treat Zone A as the receiving zone: inbound docks 1-4, unloading and goods inspection. Direct all inbound carriers to Zone A and keep outbound movements clear of its apron.

3. Reserve dock doors 1-4 for inbound receiving. Never plan inbound unloading at any other door without rescheduling through the responsible role.

4. Obtain a booked slot from the dispatcher before travelling to site. Dispatchers book transport, assign dock doors and release outbound loads.

5. Follow the door and time slot assigned by the dispatcher. The dispatcher assigns dock doors and time slots to carriers.

6. Report to the assigned inbound door at the booked time. Confirm the door number on arrival with receiving staff and wait for direction before reversing onto the leveller.

7. Present delivery notes, purchase references and any temperature or hazardous paperwork at the dock office immediately on arrival. Keep seals intact until documents have been accepted.

8. Apply the document check before unloading on every delivery. At receiving, the document check happens BEFORE unloading (PR-01).

9. Verify carrier identity, purchase order, pallet count and seal number against the booking. Record discrepancies on the arrival record and escalate to the dispatcher before breaking bulk.

10. Unload only after the document check has passed. Move pallets directly to the marked inspection lanes in Zone A and keep labels visible for counting.

11. Hold vehicles without a valid booking clear of doors 1-4 until the dispatcher provides a revised slot. Prohibit queuing across main transport routes or pedestrian crossings.

12. Close each arrival by confirming door release with receiving staff. Leave Zone A only when documents, pallets and inspection status match the PR-01 Inbound receiving record for that slot.

title: Unloading and inspection
text:
1. Execute PR-01 Inbound receiving only in Zone A at inbound docks 1-4. Confine all unloading and goods inspection to the receiving zone until goods are released for booking.

Zone A is the sole authorised point for inbound docks 1-4, unloading and goods inspection. Direct every inbound vehicle to those doors and refuse unloading at any other location.

2. Assign unloading, counting and inspection in Zone A to inbound operators. Inbound operators unload, count and inspect inbound goods in Zone A and retain custody until inspection is complete.

Permit no handover to storage or picking before that inspection is signed off. Escalate shortages, overages and visible damage through the receiving record without delay.

3. Wear high-visibility vests on the warehouse floor without exception. High-visibility vests are mandatory for everyone on the warehouse floor, including drivers under escort and visitors.

4. Wear safety footwear class S3 on the warehouse floor without exception. Safety footwear class S3 is mandatory on the warehouse floor for the full duration of PR-01 Inbound receiving.

Refuse floor access to any person missing either item of protective equipment. Stop unloading work immediately if compliance cannot be restored.

5. Complete the document check before unloading. At receiving, the document check happens BEFORE unloading.

Compare the delivery note, order reference, pallet count and carrier identity against the scheduled booking. Note any mismatch on the receiving record and hold the vehicle at the dock pending instruction.

6. Unload only after the document check is cleared. Place pallets fully inside Zone A, clear of dock edges, levellers and pedestrian routes. Keep each consignment separate and labelled with its delivery reference.

Count every pallet, carton and loose unit during unloading. Record the counted quantity independently of the quantity stated on the paperwork.

7. Inspect all inbound goods BEFORE system booking. Inbound goods are inspected BEFORE they are booked into the system.

Examine packaging integrity, labelling, quantities, variants and expiry or batch markings where applicable. Photograph defects, reseal opened checks where possible, and segregate non-conforming goods within Zone A.

8. Use the handheld WMS scanners to record receipt checks in Zone A. Pickers and inbound staff share 20 handheld WMS scanners.

Draw scanners from the shared pool at the start of PR-01 Inbound receiving and return them promptly for picking use. Scan each handling unit, confirm the counted quantity, and attach the inspection result to the receipt.

9. Release for booking only inspected and accepted goods. Forward the verified count and inspection outcome to the booking step and retain rejected or queried goods under inbound-operator control.

Prevent uninspected pallets from leaving Zone A under any circumstances. Maintain the sequence of document check, then unloading, then inspection, then system booking on every delivery.

title: Booking and release
text:
1. Complete PR-01 Inbound receiving for every delivery in Zone A before creating any system stock.

2. Assign Inbound operators unload, count and inspection duties for the delivery in Zone A. Do not split accountability for one vehicle across unbriefed staff.

Inbound operators unload, count and inspect inbound goods in Zone A. Retain that ownership from door opening until the booking decision. Hand over open checks verbally and on the scanner at task change.

3. Inspect all cartons, pallets and labels before booking. Verify quantity against the delivery note, check for damage and confirm product identity and date marks.

4. Hold inbound goods unbooked until inspection is finished. Inbound goods are inspected BEFORE they are booked into the system.

5. Segregate non-conforming quantities at the inspection point. Keep them physically separate from accepted stock and prevent release to storage.

6. Book only inspected and accepted quantities into the warehouse management system under PR-01 Inbound receiving. Record supplier, delivery note number, item code, batch, quantity and storage requirement at booking.

7. Attach labels to every pallet or handling unit immediately after booking. Scan-verify each label against the system receipt before moving the unit from the inspection area.

8. Release booked stock to PR-02 Put-away to storage without delay. Goods are booked into the system BEFORE put-away to storage.

9. Sequence inspection, system booking and put-away strictly in that order. Never stage unbooked pallets for put-away and never book pallets still awaiting inspection results.

10. Confirm system availability of the receipt before directing put-away trucks. Cancel the release if the booking fails to post and return the pallets to the holding area.

11. Direct put-away by system task only after release. State destination zone, aisle and location on each task and enforce first instruction compliance.

12. Close the PR-01 Inbound receiving receipt after all pallets are booked and released. Reconcile booked quantity to inspected quantity and report any shortfall to the stock controller for review.

Retain delivery paperwork with the receipt record for traceability. File exceptions separately and ensure put-away teams work only from confirmed system stock when executing PR-02 Put-away to storage.

title: Bulk storage put-away
text:
1. Execute every bulk movement under PR-02 Put-away to storage without deviation from the system-directed location.
2. Complete system booking before any physical put-away to storage. Goods are booked into the system BEFORE put-away to storage.
3. Direct all bulk-storage pallets to Zone B. Zone B is the bulk storage zone: high-bay pallet racking.
4. Utilise only the location assigned by the warehouse system for each pallet. The high-bay racking provides 2,400 pallet positions.
5. Confirm pallet weight against the system receipt before lifting to height. A pallet, including its load, may weigh at most 800 kg.
6. Observe the bay limit on every level during placement. Each rack bay may carry at most 2,700 kg.
7. Distribute heavy pallets to lower beam levels and never concentrate full-weight units in a single bay beyond its rating. Report any overload indication, deflection or impact damage immediately and quarantine the bay until cleared.
8. Apply free block-stack limits only where racking locations are not available and the system explicitly directs block stacking. Free block-stacked pallets must not exceed 4.0 m in height.
9. Count units in the stack as well as height. Free block-stacked pallets must not exceed 3 pallets high.
10. Align block stacks squarely, with base pallets fully supported and labels facing the aisle for scanning. Do not lean pallets against racking uprights or intrude into adjacent aisles.
11. Return damaged pallets, collapsed loads or overweight units to the inspection area for reassessment instead of forcing them into storage.
12. Log every put-away confirmation by scanner at the storage location. Investigate any mismatch between physical location and system location before leaving the aisle.
13. Protect racking integrity throughout all handling. The maintenance technician maintains MHE, racking and dock equipment and logs all repairs.
14. Notify the maintenance technician at once of any upright damage, beam deformation, missing safety pins or anchor failure observed during PR-02 Put-away to storage. Record the bay identifier, retain photographs where safe to do so, and prevent further put-away to that bay until release.
15. Support the preventive regime for storage infrastructure. Racking gets a documented safety inspection every month.

title: Cold-zone storage
text:
1. Store all chilled product requiring controlled refrigeration in Zone E under PR-12 Cold-chain handling.
2. Maintain Zone E as chilled storage held at +2 to +8 °C at all times, without exception for seasonal conditions or door activity.
3. Keep the cold zone at or above +2 °C to prevent freezing, chill injury and loss of product specification.
4. Keep the cold zone at or below +8 °C to prevent microbial growth, spoilage and breach of customer temperature requirements.
5. Verify the cold-zone temperature manually each shift with the calibrated monitoring equipment provided at the designated reading point.
6. Record each shift verification immediately in the temperature log, including the reading, time and identity of the person performing the check.
7. Restrict entry to Zone E to personnel engaged in put-away, replenishment, picking, stock counting or supervision of those tasks.
8. Minimise door open time during every movement in and out of the cold zone, and close the doors and curtains fully after each pallet transfer.
9. Transfer chilled pallets directly between the inbound inspection area and Zone E without staging in ambient areas, and move outbound chilled pallets directly to the dispatch staging area for prompt loading.
10. Arrange chilled stock to allow free air circulation around pallets, racking and evaporators, and never block sensors, fans or the manual verification point.
11. Apply stock rotation strictly in Zone E, placing incoming batches behind existing stock and picking the earliest expiry first unless the system directs otherwise.
12. Inspect chilled packaging, seals and labels for condensation damage, ice formation and legibility during put-away and before replenishment to the pick faces.
13. Respond at once to any reading outside +2 to +8 °C, any alarm, or any sign of refrigeration malfunction by quarantining affected stock and escalating through PR-12 Cold-chain handling.
14. Move pallets found outside the permitted temperature range to quarantine in the designated area for assessment, and do not return them to Zone E or release them for picking until assessment is complete.
15. Keep Zone E floors dry, clear of debris and free of standing water, since condensation and meltwater create slip and contamination risks in chilled conditions.
16. Wear the insulated protective clothing provided for extended work in Zone E, and limit continuous exposure by rotating tasks between chilled and ambient areas.
17. Report door faults, damaged seals, lighting failures, icing on floors or evaporators, and any drift in shift readings for corrective action under PR-12 Cold-chain handling.

title: Hazmat cage and quarantine
text:
1. Locate both controlled areas in Zone F. The hazmat cage is inside Zone F and the quarantine area is in Zone F.
2. Recognise the shared setting. Zone F holds the value-added services area, so separate hazmat and quarantine stock physically from all rework, labelling and kitting activity.
3. Apply PR-13 Hazmat handling and spill response to every receipt, movement, check and spill in the cage. Do not substitute local practice for that procedure.
4. Respect the size of the enclosure. The hazmat cage inside Zone F covers 60 m2. Keep its boundary clear, locked and marked at all times.
5. Enforce the weight ceiling without exception. No more than 4,000 kg of hazmat may be stored in the hazmat cage at one time.
6. Convert the ceiling into pallet planning before booking any pallet in. A pallet, including its load, may weigh at most 800 kg.
7. Calculate cage loading on full-weight units. The hazmat cage holds at most 5 full-weight pallets (hazmat stock limit divided by maximum pallet weight).
8. Record inbound weight on the system receipt and verify the running cage total before transporting any additional pallet to the cage. Reject any movement that would breach the limit.
9. Segregate incompatible classes inside the cage using the designated bays and bunds. Stack only stable, sealed and labelled units on intact pallets.
10. Inspect the cage each shift for leaks, damaged packaging, missing labels and blocked access. Report defects immediately and contain spills exactly as PR-13 Hazmat handling and spill response directs.
11. Use the quarantine area only for stock placed on system hold pending inspection, assessment or decision. Keep quarantined pallets clearly labelled and system-blocked against picking, replenishment and dispatch.
12. Prohibit direct put-away, picking or dispatch from quarantine. Move pallets out only after the authorised assessment releases them to their system-directed destination.
13. Count and secure both areas during stocktaking. Keep cage and quarantine locations closed to put-away and picking until their counts are closed.
14. Maintain separation between the two areas. Never store hazmat overflow in quarantine and never store quarantined general stock inside the hazmat cage to compensate for lack of racking space.

title: Replenishment of pick faces
text:
1. Execute PR-03 Replenishment of pick faces as the bulk to pick-face feed before picking. Complete all system-directed replenishment before the picking shift starts.

2. Draw reserve stock only from Zone B. Zone B is the bulk storage zone: high-bay pallet racking. Confirm the system-directed source location, product, batch and quantity before leaving the rack.

3. Deliver replenishment only to Zone C. Zone C is the picking zone: ground-level pick faces and flow racks. Place each unit on its assigned pick face or flow-rack lane and never substitute a neighbouring location without a new system task.

4. Maintain forward flow at all times. Pallets transfer from Zone A to Zone B to Zone C to Zone D. Return any excess or mis-directed stock to its Zone B reserve location rather than staging it in the picking aisles.

5. Assign forklift movements to authorised operators. Forklift operators operate forklifts, reach trucks and pallet jacks. Use the truck type directed for the height and aisle, and keep forks low and the load stable while travelling to Zone C.

6. Keep pick faces owned by the picking operation. Pickers pick customer orders in Zone C against scanner tasks. Do not allow replenishment pallets, wrapping material or empty pallets to block a pick face that pickers need for scanner-directed work.

7. Scan-verify every replenishment movement at both ends. Scan the source licence plate in Zone B on removal, then scan the destination pick-face label in Zone C on placement. Correct any mismatch in the system immediately and do not leave unverified stock on a pick face.

8. Top up flow racks from the rear feed side where provided. Push existing units forward, load incoming units behind them, and check that rollers, guides and lane stops move freely. Report any jammed lane, damaged beam or missing label before continuing.

9. Replenish to the directed level only. Fill the pick face to its maximum system level without overstacking, crushing cartons or overhanging the face. Remove damaged outer cartons from the feed and handle them through the damaged-goods route.

10. Sequence replenishment by picking priority. Complete urgent and short pick faces first, then complete the remaining scheduled top-ups. Coordinate with the shift team so that replenishment activity is clear of active picking before the picking shift starts.

11. Control the replenishment window under supervision. The shift supervisor runs one shift: floor staff and incident response. Escalate shortages, reserve-location empty flags, congestion in Zone C, or system faults to supervision without delay.

12. Close out PR-03 Replenishment of pick faces before releasing work to PR-04 Order picking. Confirm all replenishment tasks are completed or formally carried over, pick faces are faced up and accessible, and empty pallets and waste are removed from Zone C.

title: Order picking
text: 1. Execute all work in this section under PR-04 Order picking. 2. Confine picking activity to Zone C, the picking zone with ground-level pick faces and flow racks. 3. Assign only pickers to customer orders in Zone C, working strictly against scanner tasks. 4. Confirm completion of PR-03 Replenishment of pick faces before the picking shift starts. 5. Do not commence picking on any lane flagged short or unreplenished until replenishment is confirmed in the system. 6. Collect a handheld WMS scanner at shift start from the charging station. 7. Recognise that pickers and inbound staff share 20 handheld WMS scanners across shifts. 8. Report any scanner shortage or fault to the shift supervisor immediately and do not use paper substitutes. 9. Log on with your personal ID and accept only tasks dispatched to you. 10. Drive replenishment-before-picking discipline by checking task start time against replenishment closure for your aisle. 11. Navigate directly to the location shown on the scanner, verifying aisle, bay and level before touching stock. 12. Within Zone C, pick solely from ground-level pick faces and flow-rack lanes, never from reserve levels above. 13. Scan each source location label first, then scan every item or carton picked. 14. Follow the scanner sequence exactly, picking the quantity prompted and no more. 15. Place picked items into the designated tote, carton or cage as instructed by the task. 16. Where the flow rack shows empty rollers or a broken carton face, stop picking that location and alert the shift supervisor for urgent top-up. 17. Keep opened cartons squared, labels visible and surplus stock tucked behind the pick edge. 18. Under PR-04 Order picking, complete scan verification of picked items before transfer to packing. 19. Hand over only scan-verified picks to PR-05 Packing and labelling, ensuring picked items are scan-verified before packing. 20. Never bypass a failed scan, force-close a short pick or re-enter quantities manually without supervisor instruction. 21. For any short, damaged or mis-labelled pick face, record the exception in the scanner and move to the next task. 22. Return the scanner tote closure promptly at task end, confirm the tote ID and leave completed totes in the marked collection point. 23. Maintain clear pick faces and flow-rack approaches, removing stretch film, strapping and empty cartons to waste cages. 24. Return the handheld scanner to charge at break and shift end, logging off so the next picker or inbound operator can draw from the shared pool of 20 units.

title: Packing and labelling
text:
1. Execute PR-05 Packing and labelling for every outbound order in Zone D before transfer to loading.
2. Maintain Zone D as the dispatch zone: outbound staging in front of docks 5-8, kept clear for packed pallets only.
3. Accept totes and pallets into packing only from completed PR-04 Order picking tasks with intact source documentation.
4. Scan-verify each picked item BEFORE packing, and do not start carton build, labelling or wrapping until verification passes in the system.
5. Reject any unverified, short-picked or damaged item from the pack station and return it through the defined correction route.
6. Select the system-directed carton, tote or pallet configuration for the order and check weight distribution before filling.
7. Apply handling, address and system-generated despatch labels flat, legible and scannable, with one principal label per handling unit.
8. Confirm label data against the outbound load record before sealing, including destination, handling unit count and service marking.
9. Seal cartons and stabilise palletised loads immediately after packing to prevent movement during staging.
10. Wrap all outbound pallets on the 2 semi-automatic stretch wrappers in dispatch, using the specified wrap pattern for the load type.
11. Inspect wrapped pallets for overhang, punctured film, loose layers or obscured labels and rewrap any non-conforming pallet at once.
12. Stage finished, scan-verified and wrapped pallets in Zone D by outbound door 5-8 in load sequence, labels facing the aisle.
13. Keep packing waste, spare cartons and consumables away from staged loads and remove them continuously during the shift.
14. Hand over staged loads only to PR-06 Outbound dispatch, with dispatchers booking transport, assigning dock doors and releasing outbound loads.
15. Record packed handling units, labels issued and pallets wrapped in the system before releasing the staging lane for loading.

title: Staging and loading
text:
1. Execute PR-06 Outbound dispatch only in the designated dispatch footprint.
Zone D is the dispatch zone: outbound staging in front of docks 5-8. Keep all staged pallets, totes and loading equipment inside the marked Zone D lanes. Never overspill staging into travel aisles or pedestrian routes.

2. Confirm release status before moving any load to the doors.
Dispatchers book transport, assign dock doors and release outbound loads. Move a staging lane to a door only after the dispatcher has released that outbound load in the system. Reject verbal release requests from drivers or other staff.

3. Use only the assigned door and time slot.
The dispatcher assigns dock doors and time slots to carriers. Position the trailer or vehicle at the door stated on the dispatch plan. Dock doors 5-8 serve outbound dispatch; never load an outbound trailer at inbound doors.

4. Prepare the door, vehicle and leveller before loading starts.
Apply the vehicle brakes, fit wheel chocks and confirm the vehicle is stationary at the door. Each of the 8 dock doors has a dock leveller; inspect the assigned leveller for damage or obstruction and confirm stable seating of the lip on the trailer bed. Report defects at once and do not load across an unsafe leveller.

5. Stage loads in door order and keep lanes identifiable.
Arrange wrapped pallets and packed units in the Zone D staging lane in reverse loading order, with door number, route and seal reference visible on the lane marker. Leave clear access for the pre-departure check and for emergency egress. Do not double-stack staging unless the load plan explicitly permits it.

6. Control forklift speed on ramps and leveller approaches.
Drive at walking pace through the door area and give way to banksmen where assigned. Forklifts must not exceed 5 km/h on dock ramps and leveller approaches. Square the forks to the leveller, cross the plate centrally without turning, and stop fully before raising or lowering the load.

7. Load against the system sequence and verify every unit.
Scan each pallet or handling unit as it crosses onto the trailer and reconcile the count against the outbound load record. Stop loading immediately on any scan mismatch, short pallet or damaged wrapping and notify the dispatcher. Never substitute pallets from another lane to complete a load.

8. Secure, seal and document the trailer before departure.
Fit load restraints, close and lock the trailer doors, and apply the recorded seal. Enter the seal number, door number, departure time and loader identity in the outbound record. Photograph the sealed doors where the dispatch plan requires evidence.

9. Maintain control during interruptions and evacuation.
Halt all loading activity if the fire alarm sounds and follow PR-14 Emergency evacuation without moving trailers or removing levellers under load. Roll call at the assembly point happens BEFORE anyone re-enters the building. Resume PR-06 Outbound dispatch only after authorised re-entry, then re-verify the open door, vehicle position and staged count before continuing.

title: Load and capacity limits
text:
1. Apply this section to every load planned and released under PR-06 Outbound dispatch.
2. Limit each pallet, including its load, to at most 800 kg.
3. Weigh or verify any suspect pallet before staging and remove overweight units from the outbound lane.
4. Plan contracted curtain-side trailers on a payload of 22000 kg.
5. Use 33 floor pallet positions as the physical floor limit for a trailer.
6. Load at most 27 full-weight pallets per trailer, determined by payload divided by maximum pallet weight and capped by floor positions.
7. Check both weight and floor positions on every trailer plan and apply the lower resulting limit.
8. Plan mixed lighter pallets against the same payload and floor limits and never exceed either constraint.
9. Plan the delivery van on a payload of 1200 kg.
10. Use 6 pallet positions as the physical floor limit for the delivery van.
11. Load at most 1 full-weight pallets in the van.
12. Transfer any heavier van order to trailer despatch and do not split a full-weight pallet across vehicles.
13. Schedule each outbound door for 3 trailer loads per shift.
14. Operate with 4 outbound dock doors for outbound planning.
15. Cap outbound capacity at 324 full-weight pallets per shift, calculated as doors x loads per shift x pallets per trailer.
16. Sequence door bookings to spread heavy pallets across loads and doors.
17. Reject any loading plan that exceeds trailer payload, van payload, floor positions, full-weight pallet maxima or the per-shift capacity.
18. Recalculate the plan when pallet weights change after wrapping, labelling or late additions.
19. Instruct loaders to stop loading when the verified weight or count reaches the applicable limit.
20. Record the final pallet count and gross weight for each released load in the system.

Under PR-06 Outbound dispatch weight governs before floor space where pallets are at maximum weight. A trailer offering 33 floor positions therefore departs full by weight at 27 full-weight pallets. Apply the same logic to the van, where payload restricts the van to 1 full-weight pallets despite 6 pallet positions.

Across 4 outbound dock doors at 3 trailer loads per shift, the site limit of 324 full-weight pallets per shift protects dock throughput, labour planning and vehicle availability. Build the daily despatch schedule backward from that ceiling. Prioritise timed collections within the ceiling and roll excess quantity to the next available load.

Validate every exception against pallet weight and trailer or van capacity before authorising an additional vehicle. Retain load calculations with the outbound documentation for traceability.

title: MHE fleet
text:
1. Operate all mechanical handling equipment only under PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation.
2. Forklift operators operate forklifts, reach trucks and pallet jacks.
3. Assign only trained and authorised operators to powered trucks for any shift task.
4. The electric counterbalance fleet comprises 6 electric counterbalance forklifts.
5. Each counterbalance forklift is rated at 2.5 t; never exceed the rated capacity plate during lifting, travelling or stacking.
6. Deploy counterbalance trucks for receiving, dispatch, yard transfers and general horizontal transport.
7. The high-bay fleet comprises 4 reach trucks for the high bays.
8. Each reach truck is rated at 1.6 t; respect load centres, lift heights and bay limits when placing pallets in racking.
9. Reserve reach trucks for narrow-aisle work in bulk storage and for replenishment movements to and from reserve locations.
10. The pallet jack fleet comprises 8 electric pallet jacks for powered horizontal movement.
11. Supplement powered movement with 12 hand pallet jacks distributed for picking support, staging and short transfers.
12. Select the smallest suitable truck for each movement; use pallet jacks for ground-level transfers and retain counterbalance and reach capacity for lifting and longer hauls.
13. Report any loss of lifting performance, steering, braking, horn, lights, battery condition or structural damage before further use.
14. Complete the documented pre-use check for every forklift each day.
15. Perform the daily forklift check BEFORE first use each day; do not start the truck, move a load or leave the park area until the check is recorded as passed.
16. Extend the same daily discipline to reach trucks and electric pallet jacks; quarantine any unit that fails and attach a clear do-not-use notice.
17. Park defective equipment in the designated quarantine line and notify supervision immediately for reassignment of work.
18. The maintenance technician maintains MHE, racking and dock equipment and logs all repairs.
19. Enter every defect, service action, battery change and component replacement in the maintenance log; retain check sheets for audit and trend review.
20. Remove from service any truck with overdue planned maintenance until the maintenance technician returns it to use.
21. Charge electric trucks only in designated charging positions; secure cables, confirm ventilation and leave hand pallet jacks clear of aisles and walkways.
22. Pickers and inbound staff share 20 handheld WMS scanners for put-away, replenishment, picking and receiving transactions.
23. Collect a fully charged scanner at shift start, verify login and scan function, and return the unit to charge at shift end.
24. Handle scanners as operational equipment; report faults immediately so a spare can be issued without stopping put-away or picking flow.

title: Aisles and speed limits
text:
1. Keep main transport aisles clear at all times for two-way truck movement. Main transport aisles are 4.0 m wide. Do not stage pallets, waste, charging equipment or packing materials in them.

2. Reserve rack storage aisles for put-away, replenishment and picking movements only. Rack storage aisles are 3.0 m wide. Enter them only when your task requires it and exit promptly when finished.

3. Use segregated pedestrian walkways for all foot movement alongside traffic routes. Segregated pedestrian walkways are 1.2 m wide. Do not walk outside them where a segregated route is provided.

4. Apply PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation and PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse on all aisles, crossings and yard routes. Give way to pedestrians at every marked crossing and maintain clear sightlines at intersections.

5. Do not exceed 8 km/h inside the building. Adjust speed further for load weight, aisle width, visibility and floor conditions. Stop completely where sightlines are blocked and sound the horn before proceeding.

6. Do not exceed 15 km/h in the outdoor yard. Keep to defined traffic lanes, watch for parked trailers and dock manoeuvres, and increase following distances in wet or low-light conditions.

7. Slow to 5 km/h in marked pedestrian zones and crossings. Approach at walking pace, make eye contact with pedestrians where possible, and stop if any person enters the travel path.

8. Do not exceed 5 km/h on dock ramps and leveller approaches. Square up to the leveller, centre the load, and cross steadily without turning, braking harshly or accelerating on the incline.

9. Never overtake another truck in a rack storage aisle, on a dock ramp or leveller approach, or in a marked pedestrian zone. Wait until both trucks are back in a main transport aisle with clear visibility.

10. Keep pedestrian walkways physically separated from truck routes. Do not narrow the 1.2 m clear width with pallets, totes, stretch film or strapping. Remove any obstruction immediately and report damage to markings or barriers.

11. Park only in designated positions clear of aisles and walkways. Switch off and secure the truck, lower the forks, and leave sufficient clearance for passing traffic and emergency access.

12. Report faded floor markings, damaged signage, obstructed crossings or faulty lighting without delay. Do not operate at normal aisle speeds where markings or visibility are impaired until the route is restored.

title: Dock and packing equipment
text:
1. Keep all dock and packing equipment ready for PR-05 Packing and labelling and PR-06 Outbound dispatch throughout both shifts.
2. Packing under PR-05 is executed in Zone D before transfer to loading; operate the wrapping and baling equipment only in its designated positions.
3. Dispatch uses 2 semi-automatic stretch wrappers.
4. Outbound pallet stretch wrappers are located in dispatch in Zone D; move only wrapped pallets from the wrappers to staging.
5. Check the wrapper turntable, film carriage and controls for damage or film breaks before starting each wrapping run.
6. Thread film strictly to the posted diagram on each machine; cut and secure the film tail on completion of every pallet.
7. Isolate a wrapper at once on unusual noise, uneven wrapping or control failure and notify the maintenance technician.
8. The site has 1 cardboard baler; feed only flattened cardboard from unpacking and picking waste through the baler.
9. Compress material in full cycles, tie off each bale before ejection and keep hands clear of the press chamber during operation.
10. Store finished bales clear of wrapper lanes, staging lanes and dock approaches until collection.
11. Each of the 8 dock doors has a dock leveller; the building has 8 dock doors, with dock doors 1-4 serving inbound receiving and dock doors 5-8 serving outbound dispatch.
12. Deploy the dock leveller only after the vehicle is braked, chocked and confirmed stationary at the door.
13. Operate dock levellers in order: check for damage or obstruction, then position and extend the lip, then confirm stable seating before movements.
14. Confirm the lip rests fully on the vehicle bed and the deck sits level before driving pallet equipment across.
15. Return each leveller to its stored position and close the dock door immediately after the vehicle departs.
16. Report bent lips, sticking decks, oil leaks, missing edge guards or obstructed pits to the maintenance technician without delay.
17. The maintenance technician maintains MHE, racking and dock equipment and logs all repairs; do not attempt electrical, hydraulic or structural repairs to wrappers, the baler or levellers.
18. Tag defective equipment out of use, record the door or unit number and fault observed, and hand the record to supervision for action.

title: Forklift operation
text:
1. Apply PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation to every forklift movement inside the building and in the outdoor yard.
2. Restrict driving of forklifts, reach trucks and pallet jacks to designated forklift operators only, as forklift operators operate forklifts, reach trucks and pallet jacks.
3. Obtain authorisation before operating any truck for the first time, since only the warehouse manager may authorise new forklift operators.
4. Present licences, certificates and site induction records to the warehouse manager for assessment before authorisation.

Do not drive without current authorisation recorded by the warehouse manager, even under supervision.
5. Complete the documented pre-use check on every forklift each day under PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation.
6. Carry out the daily forklift check before first use each day and rectify any defect before starting work.

Record the check in the daily log, sign it, and park any truck with brake, steering, horn, light, tyre or fork defects for repair.
7. Fasten the seat belt before moving off and keep it fastened whenever the truck is moving.

Stop the truck, re-apply the belt if released for load adjustment, and proceed only with the belt secured.
8. Limit speed to 8 km/h inside the building on all internal routes.
9. Restrict speed to 15 km/h in the outdoor yard and adjust further for weather, surface and visibility.
10. Slow to 5 km/h in marked pedestrian zones and crossings and give way to pedestrians at all times.
11. Hold speed to 5 km/h on dock ramps and leveller approaches and approach levellers squarely without sharp turns.

Sound the horn on blind corners, at crossings and before reversing, and maintain safe separation from other trucks and pedestrians.
12. Carry only stable, secured loads within rated capacity, keep forks low during travel, and tilt back slightly for stability.
13. Stop immediately for any pedestrian in the travel path, any obstruction, or any loss of visibility.

Report near misses, impacts, equipment faults and speed-limit breaches promptly, and do not resume driving until cleared where required under PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation.

title: Pedestrian safety
text:
1. Apply PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse on every movement on foot inside the building and in the outdoor yard.
2. Use only marked segregated walkways and marked crossings for pedestrian access to receiving, storage, picking and dispatch areas.
3. Keep to the segregated pedestrian walkways, which are 1.2 m wide, and walk in single file where the marking requires it.
4. Do not step into main transport aisles except at marked crossings, as main transport aisles are 4.0 m wide and carry two-way truck traffic.
5. Enter rack storage aisles on foot only where the task requires it, noting that rack storage aisles are 3.0 m wide and leave limited clearance around operating trucks.
6. Stop at the edge of every marked crossing, look both ways, and make eye contact with the approaching driver before stepping out.
7. Give way to all moving materials handling equipment at crossings, junctions and dock approaches, even where pedestrians have a marked path.
8. Expect forklifts to slow to 5 km/h in marked pedestrian zones and crossings, and do not assume the driver has seen you until the truck has visibly slowed.
9. Observe the site speed regime when judging gaps to cross: forklifts must not exceed 8 km/h inside the building, forklifts must not exceed 15 km/h in the outdoor yard, and forklifts must not exceed 5 km/h on dock ramps and leveller approaches.
10. Keep clear of dock ramps, leveller approaches and the swing path of dock doors and leveller lips during loading and unloading.
11. Never walk under raised forks, raised loads or an extended leveller lip, and never climb over pallets, stretch film or strapping left in a walkway.
12. Wear a high-visibility vest at all times on the warehouse floor, since high-visibility vests are mandatory for everyone on the warehouse floor.
13. Wear compliant foot protection on every warehouse task, as safety footwear class S3 is mandatory on the warehouse floor.
14. Report faded walkway lines, damaged barriers, blocked crossings or obscured signage to the shift supervisor without delay.
15. Challenge any pedestrian observed outside the segregated system and direct them back to the nearest 1.2 m walkway.
16. Brief visitors and new starters on PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse before they enter the floor, including the 5 km/h truck limit at crossings, the 8 km/h indoor limit, the 15 km/h yard limit and the 5 km/h limit on dock ramps.
17. Stop work in the affected area if a walkway is obstructed and restore the segregated route before resuming pedestrian access.

title: PPE
text:
1. Wear a fastened high-visibility vest at all times while on the warehouse floor.
High-visibility vests are mandatory for everyone on the warehouse floor.
2. Keep the vest as the outermost garment so reflective bands remain fully visible from front, sides and rear.
Replace soiled, torn or faded vests before starting work under PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse.
3. Wear safety footwear class S3 whenever present on the warehouse floor.
Safety footwear class S3 is mandatory on the warehouse floor.
4. Lace and close S3 footwear fully before entering Zone A, Zone B, Zone C, Zone D, Zone E or Zone F.
Do not modify guards, soles or lacing systems, and withdraw damaged pairs from service immediately.
5. Fasten the forklift seat belt before moving any truck under PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation.
Forklift operators must wear seat belts whenever the truck is moving.
6. Confirm belt retraction, buckle engagement and snug fit during the daily check before first use.
Park the truck in the designated quarantine line and notify the maintenance technician if any belt is cut, frayed, jammed or fails to latch.
7. Apply these requirements to all duties without exception.
Inbound operators, pickers, forklift operators, stock controllers, returns staff, dispatchers, maintenance technicians, supervisors and escorted visitors shall comply identically during Shift 1 and Shift 2.
8. Brief every visitor and new starter on vest, footwear and belt rules before floor entry.
Issue compliant vests and confirm compliant footwear at the briefing point, and refuse floor access where either item is missing.
9. Enforce continuous use across travelling, loading, picking and supervision tasks.
Remain vested and shod while crossing marked pedestrian zones, using the 1.2 m segregated walkways, working around docks 1-8, or riding as a trained operator on counterbalance forklifts, reach trucks and electric pallet jacks.
10. Stop work affected by missing or defective PPE and correct it at once.
Direct any person without a vest, without S3 footwear, or with an unfastened seat belt on a moving truck to stop, and allow resumption only after full compliance is restored.
11. Store personal vests and footwear clean, dry and ready for the next shift.
Keep spare compliant items available at the charging station area so scanner collection, tote handling and handover activities never proceed without mandatory protection.

title: Cycle counts
text:
1. Execute this section under PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts for all daily inventory verification. Stock controllers own inventory accuracy: cycle counts, recounts and adjustments.

2. Cycle counts run every working day on a rotating zone schedule. Maintain the rotation so every storage location is counted at its planned interval without omitting any area.

3. Release the daily count list from the system at the start of the count window. Assign defined location ranges to named stock controllers and record the assignment in the count log.

4. Collect a serviceable handheld scanner from the charging pool before starting. Pickers and inbound staff share 20 handheld WMS scanners, so coordinate issue and return to avoid shortages during parallel tasks.

5. Scan each location label first, then scan every item or carton in that location. Count cartons, inner packs and loose units separately where the system requires separate quantity fields.

6. Enter the first count directly into the scanner against the directed location. Never transcribe counts on paper for later entry unless the system is unavailable and the fallback is authorised.

7. Keep counted locations free from other movements while the count remains open. Request put-away and picking operators to stand clear until you close and confirm the location.

8. Compare the first count to the system quantity immediately after entry. Where the quantities agree, close the location and proceed to the next directed location.

9. Recount every variance with a second independent count. A second count happens BEFORE any stock adjustment is posted. Perform the recount without viewing the first count quantity where the system supports blind recount.

10. Investigate persistent differences before adjustment. Check adjacent locations for misplacement, verify open replenishment and picking tasks, and review recent receipts and dispatches for the same product.

11. Post the adjustment only after the recount is complete and documented. Record the reason code, both count quantities, the scanner identity and the operator identity for each adjusted location.

12. Return the scanner to charge at the end of the count session and confirm undamaged return. Report any fault, battery failure or scanning error immediately so a replacement unit can be issued.

13. File the daily count record with first counts, recounts, adjustments and open variances. Carry unresolved variances forward to the next working day and escalate repeated discrepancies for review.

title: Annual stocktake
text:
1. Execute this section under PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts for the annual wall-to-wall stocktake.
2. Stock controllers own inventory accuracy: cycle counts, recounts and adjustments. Assign a stock controller to lead preparation, counting control and reconciliation for the full event.
3. Schedule a full wall-to-wall stocktake once a year. Publish the date, frozen zones and shift plan in advance so receiving, put-away, picking and dispatch can be paused or sequenced.
4. Freeze all system movements for the zones under count. Prohibit put-away, replenishment, picking, booking and adjustments in the frozen area until the count for that area is closed.
5. Brief all counters on scan method, location sequence and variance handling before starting. Issue calibrated scanners and confirm each operator understands the location label sequence.
6. Count every pallet position, pick face, bulk location and system-directed quarantine location on a wall-to-wall basis. Record each location as counted, empty or inaccessible, and leave no location unchecked.
7. Enter first counts directly into the scanner at the location. Do not use paper transcription unless the system is unavailable and the authorised fallback applies.
8. Compare first counts to system stock immediately after each area is closed. Direct the second count team to every location with a variance, damaged label or unreadable identifier.
9. Perform a second count BEFORE any stock adjustment is posted. Keep counted locations clear of put-away and picking until the recount is closed and reconciled.
10. Investigate persistent variances with goods inspection, document checks and movement history. Confirm misplaced pallets, open handling units and booking errors before proposing any adjustment.
11. Prepare the stocktake results pack with first-count quantities, second-count quantities, reason codes and operator identities for each adjustment. Present unresolved variances carried forward with clear ownership and deadline.
12. Submit the results pack for final sign-off. Only the warehouse manager may sign off stocktake results.
13. Release frozen zones only after sign-off or authorised partial release. Confirm the system reflects approved adjustments before restarting inbound booking, put-away and order picking.
14. File the signed results, adjustment records and variance log as the audit record for PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts. Use the findings to correct locations, labels and master data, and to improve the next annual wall-to-wall stocktake.

title: Adjustments and racking
text:
1. Stock controllers own inventory accuracy: cycle counts, recounts and adjustments across all storage locations.
2. Complete a second count before any stock adjustment is posted under PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts.
3. Never post an adjustment on a first count alone, even when the variance appears obvious from system stock or pick-face availability.
4. Record the approved recount result as the basis for the adjustment, retaining both count quantities in the system history for audit.
5. Route every adjustment arising from damage through PR-09 Damaged-goods handling before posting it against inventory.
6. Segregate the affected stock physically and systematically while the PR-09 Damaged-goods handling assessment is completed.
7. Obtain approval for the damaged-goods write-off before posting the corresponding stock adjustment.
8. Submit write-offs up to 500 EUR to the shift supervisor for approval and posting authority.
9. Escalate write-offs above 500 EUR to the warehouse manager for approval, since that threshold requires higher authority.
10. Do not split a single damage event into smaller values to remain below the approval threshold.
11. Verify racking condition during every count round, noting upright impacts, beam deflection, missing pins and load distribution.
12. Respect the limit of 2,700 kg for each rack bay when confirming quantities during recounts and adjustments.

Adjustments must correct the system to verified physical reality, not to expected levels. Where recounts confirm overstock against pallets stored above bay limits, redistribute the load before posting the adjustment.

13. Report any damaged or overloaded bay found during counting to the maintenance technician at once and block that bay from further use.
14. Ensure the maintenance technician maintains racking and dock equipment and logs all repairs arising from count findings.
15. Support the documented racking safety inspection every month by making locations accessible and highlighting suspect bays.
16. Do not use the monthly inspection as a substitute for immediate reporting between inspections; escalate defects on discovery.
17. Hold unresolved adjustment items open to the next count cycle where recount evidence remains inconclusive, rather than forcing the balance.
18. Confirm that approved adjustments are reflected in the system before releasing affected locations back to put-away or picking.

title: Returns handling
text:
1. Execute all return receipts under PR-07 Returns handling and accept no return outside the stated eligibility rule.
2. Accept returns within 14 days of delivery only and reject later arrivals through the defined exception route.
3. Verify the delivery date, customer reference and reason code against the system record before moving the goods inward.
4. Direct every authorised return immediately to Zone F for inspection and allow no diversion to storage or picking.
5. Understand that Zone F holds the value-added services area and provides the controlled space for returns assessment, rework decisions and segregated holding.
6. Returns are inspected in Zone F and no inspection activity for returns takes place in any other zone.
7. Unload and segregate inbound returns by customer, order and reason code to preserve traceability throughout PR-07 Returns handling.
8. Assign each return to trained returns staff and prevent unsupervised sorting or disposition by other roles.
9. Returns staff inspect returns in Zone F and propose restock, rework or scrap for every line inspected.
10. Examine packaging, labelling, quantity, condition and expiry where applicable and record findings directly in the system.
11. Photograph damaged, incomplete or mislabelled returns and attach the evidence to the inspection record.
12. Inspect returns BEFORE any restock, rework or scrap decision and prohibit early movement to stock or waste.
13. Grade each unit as restockable, reworkable or scrap based on the inspection result and the customer agreement.
14. Propose restock only for clean, complete, saleable units with intact labels and remaining shelf life.
15. Propose rework for units requiring cleaning, relabelling, repacking or component replacement within Zone F.
16. Propose scrap for contaminated, damaged beyond repair, incomplete or otherwise unsaleable units.
17. Submit every proposed disposition to the shift supervisor without delay and hold the goods pending approval.
18. The shift supervisor approves the final disposition of inspected returns and no restock, rework or scrap proceeds without that approval.
19. Execute approved restock movements through the system-directed destination and confirm system booking on completion.
20. Transfer approved rework units to the designated rework holding position inside Zone F and raise the rework task.
21. Isolate approved scrap units in the designated scrap holding position and prevent mixing with saleable stock.
22. Update the returns record with quantities restocked, reworked or scrapped, operator identity and approval details.
23. Notify the customer record and credit process where required once disposition is complete and approved.

title: Damaged goods
text:
1. Apply PR-09 Damaged-goods handling to every crushed carton, leaking unit, collapsed pallet, water-affected pack and suspected contamination found on receipt, in storage, at picking or on return.
2. Move the affected stock to the quarantine area in Zone F on the same shift it is found, keeping pallet integrity and labels intact for assessment.
3. Record the date, location found, product code, quantity, damage type, photographs where required, and the discovering operator in the system quarantine record.
4. Segregate damaged units from saleable stock inside quarantine, preventing any put-away, replenishment, picking or dispatch until assessment is complete.
5. Assign assessment without delay to trained personnel on the shift, preserving cold-chain or hazmat controls during the transfer where applicable.
6. Returns staff inspect returns in Zone F and propose restock, rework or scrap, completing that inspection BEFORE any restock, rework or scrap decision is taken.
7. Assess all other damaged goods on the same basis: confirm quantity and condition first, then recommend restock to saleable locations, rework in the designated area, or scrap with stated reason.
8. Obtain written write-off approval before scrapping or adjusting any value from inventory, attaching the assessment and supporting evidence to the request.
9. Send write-offs valued up to 500 EUR to the shift supervisor for approval, providing the quarantine reference, quantities and calculated value.
10. Escalate damaged-goods write-offs above 500 EUR to the warehouse manager for approval, since damaged-goods write-offs above 500 EUR need warehouse-manager approval and must not proceed on lower authority.
11. Confirm that the shift supervisor approves damaged-goods write-offs up to 500 EUR and the warehouse manager approves damaged-goods write-offs above 500 EUR, routing each case strictly by its total value.
